newsitem.title: USA: Pfizer says Aricept has fewer side effects.
newsitem.headline: Pfizer says Aricept has fewer side effects.

text.p: Pfizer Inc said on Tuesday the newly-approved drug to treat symptoms of Alzheimer's disease, Aricept, is easier to use and has fewer side effects than Warner-Lambert Co's Cognex.
Earlier Pfizer's strategic partner, Japan's Eisai Co Ltd, received approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for Aricept.

Pat Kelly, group vice president of disease management at Pfizer, said Aricept may be the second Alzheimer's drug approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration but it is the first "useful" treatment available.
He told Reuters in an interview that Cognex must be taken four times a day, rather than Aricept's single daily dose, and has serious side effects related to liver toxicity.
"Because all these effects...have all made (Cognex) a very difficult product for anyone to use, we believe Aricept represents the first real useful treatment," Kelly said.
A Warner-Lambert spokesman said he would not comment on a rival's drug but considered it a positive development to have more Alzheimer treatments available.
Kelly said Aricept, which slows down the cognitive deterioration of Alzheimer's, will be widely available in the United States shortly after the new year.
He declined to disclose the company's expectations for U.S. or global sales of Aricept.
"Pfizer doesn't reveal the specific sales expectations of any of its products," he said.
Of the four million Americans believed to suffer from the brain disorder, Kelly said about three million patients have the mild to moderate form that Aricept treats.
Pfizer's comments follow news that its strategic partner, Japan's Eisai Co Ltd, received approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for Aricept.
As part of the Eisai alliance, Pfizer will co-promote the drug in the U.S. and several other markets in Europe and Japan.
The company's promotion of the drug will include offering diagnostic tools for physicians and caretakers to spot and monitor the disease's damage to memory and cognitive abilities, Kelly said.
Kelly said Aricept is not a cure for the disease and has not been shown to have an effect on the underlying cause of Alzheimer's.
He said Pfizer and Eisai are continuing their research to treat the disease.
